title: Find the commit that broke it, in seven steps out of a hundred
summary: Something worked in the release and is broken now. Instead of reading a hundred commits, binary-search them: git bisect finds the culprit in log₂(n) tests.
mental_model: Bisect needs two facts — a commit where it worked and one where it does not — and a way to test. It then checks out the midpoint, you answer good or bad, and it halves the range until one commit is left.

write.content:
from pricing import total

assert total(100) == 120.0, 'total(100) should be 120.0, got %r' % total(100)
print('ok')

steps.title: Confirm it is broken now, and worked then
steps.why: Bisect is only as good as your two endpoints. Verify both before starting, or you will spend seven tests searching a range that does not contain the bug.
steps.expect: An AssertionError: the total is no longer 120.0.

steps.title: Check the known-good release
steps.why: Checking out the tag and running the test proves the endpoint. This is the step people skip, and it is why bisect sometimes 'finds' an innocent commit.
steps.expect: ok — it genuinely worked at v1.0.

steps.title: Start the search
steps.why: `bisect start` then `bad` and `good` define the range. Git immediately checks out the midpoint on a detached HEAD and tells you how many steps remain.
steps.expect: Roughly three steps remaining, and HEAD detached at the midpoint.

steps.title: Test the midpoint and answer
steps.why: Run the check and tell git the answer. Each answer halves the remaining range — this is the whole algorithm, and it is why a hundred commits take seven tests.

actions.run: sh -c 'python check.py > /dev/null 2>&1 && git bisect good || git bisect bad'

steps.expect: Git moves to the next midpoint and reports the remaining count.

steps.title: Keep answering until it converges
steps.why: Repeating the same conditional is exactly what `bisect run` automates in the next scenario. Here you can watch the range shrink by hand.

actions.run: sh -c 'python check.py > /dev/null 2>&1 && git bisect good || git bisect bad'
sh -c 'python check.py > /dev/null 2>&1 && git bisect good || git bisect bad'
sh -c 'python check.py > /dev/null 2>&1 && git bisect good || git bisect bad'

steps.expect: '<sha> is the first bad commit', with its full message and diff.

steps.title: Read the verdict
steps.why: Bisect writes the answer to `refs/bisect/bad` when it converges. The commit is 'Include shipping in the total' — correct, and found without reading any of the unrelated commits.
steps.expect: The shipping commit named as the culprit.

verify.label: bisect identified the commit that broke the total
verify.hint: answer good/bad at each step until it converges

steps.title: Stop bisecting and go back to work
steps.why: `bisect reset` returns you to the branch you started from and clears the state. Forgetting it leaves you on a detached HEAD, which is the usual cause of 'my changes disappeared' half an hour later.

verify.label: you are back on main with the bisect state cleared
the bisect was reset and you are back on your branch
verify.hint: git bisect reset when you are done

verify.label: no bisect state was left behind
history is untouched — bisect only reads, it never changes anything
the culprit commit is identifiable by name for the follow-up fix

pitfalls: Verify both endpoints before starting. A 'good' commit that was already broken sends bisect into the wrong half entirely.
During a bisect you are on a detached HEAD. Commit nothing; `git bisect reset` first.
If a commit cannot be tested — it does not build, for instance — answer `git bisect skip` rather than guessing.
`git bisect log > file` and `git bisect replay file` let you save and resume a search, which matters when each test takes ten minutes.
Bisect assumes the bug appeared once and stayed. A flaky test makes it converge confidently on an innocent commit.
cheatsheet: stop and return to your branch
